title: Abstract asserts the gate failure 'points to a defect in the pipeline'; Section 4.6 says this was never tested and Related Work gives a benign explanation
quote: reference solutions lowers pass@1 by 32.2 points, which points to a de-
explanation: The abstract states as an inference that the gate failure indicates a pipeline defect. Section 4.6 says only that 'We noticed the shift to the reference style but did not test it as the cause; a collapse of this size ... is also what a pipeline defect would produce'. That is a statement of compatibility, not evidence. Section 2 cites Kim et al. and says that self-distillation 'can cut accuracy, as our train-on-gold control does', which treats the gold collapse as a known, non-defect phenomenon. Section 4.4 offers a third reading, 'generic SFT damage fits as well'. So the paper holds three incompatible stories (defect, known SFT-on-solutions degradation, generic SFT damage) and picks the first in the abstract. No pipeline check is reported: no sanity run, no inspection of the gold-arm training data or tokenisation, no check that gold-trained outputs are scored correctly. The abstract's causal step 'gate fails -> pipeline defect -> null concerns this recipe only' is therefore unsupported.
related_sections: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: Train-on-gold is not a valid positive gate: it changes output format, which both graders depend on, and the paper's own citation says such SFT can lower accuracy
quote: a positive gate that must raise accuracy for the recipe to count as able to help.
explanation: The gate's success criterion is that SFT on 300 reference solutions must raise pass@1 of an already heavily post-trained instruct model. That is not a reasonable expectation. Reference solutions differ in style from the model's own output ($-delimited spans, much shorter responses, no \boxed as prompted). The paper reports the model converts to this style (60 -> 1,577 of 1,600 generations; 5% -> 98% earlier) and that response length halves. Both the selecting verifier and the 'independent' grader (last \boxed string match) key on \boxed, so a model that stops boxing scores lower under either grader without any loss of mathematical ability. The gate therefore mostly measures format transfer, not whether the recipe can help. Self-training on the model's own outputs does not shift format this way, so the gate does not stand in for the loop. Treating the gate as a validity precondition and then declaring the recipe 'not validated' is a stronger conclusion than the gate supports. The paper never checks whether gold-trained models still give correct answers in a form that neither grader credits (4.4 admits the 14% unboxed generations are 'not covered').
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: The 'recipe' null is gated only at the highest rate (and on a different recipe in the final round); no gate exists for the 1e-5 / 1e-4 runs that carry the main null
quote: No arm improves, not even training on reference
explanation: The Introduction and Contributions conclude that, because even train-on-gold does not improve, the null concerns the recipe. In Design I the train-on-gold arm exists only at 5e-4 (Table 3), where every arm declines. The headline null is at 1e-5 (k=8, 5 rounds) and 1e-4. The gate there is absent: it would plausibly not collapse at 1e-5, so 'even gold does not improve' is untested at the rates the main claim covers. The only other gate (final round) belongs to a different recipe (completion-only loss, all-linear LoRA, 1,024 cap, 300 MATH-train pool, k=2, one adapter). The inference from 'a gate fails' to 'the recipe in Tables 1-2 cannot help' therefore borrows a failure from other configurations. Which 'recipe' the title and abstract refer to is also ambiguous: the original (Design I) or the revised one.
related_sections: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: 'Revised recipe' targeted the suspected causes, so a failed gate undercuts the 'null for the recipe' reading rather than supporting it
quote: the recipe (LoRA on q/v projections, loss over the prompt, a 512-token limit)
explanation: Section 4.4 says the nulls 'may reflect the recipe' and lists these three features as suspects. Section 4.6 changes exactly those (completion-only loss, all-linear LoRA, 1,024 cap) and the gate still fails at 1e-4 and 2e-5. This shows the failure is not due to those suspected recipe features. What is left is a harness defect, a format artifact of gold-style SFT, or something about the data. If it is a harness defect, the loop results from the same pipeline (including the −4.1 mean decline) are also suspect, and the 'null concerns this recipe only' scoping becomes 'the pipeline is unvalidated', which is broader. The Conclusion ('lowers pass@1 by about 30 points even with a revised recipe, this is a null for the recipe') still treats the recipe as the unit of the null. The paper also keeps the final-round loop decline as a headline result in the abstract, Section 5.1 and the Conclusion, while saying the revised recipe cannot be validated and seven changes were made at once with no ablation.
related_sections: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: Controls described as having 'no verifier at all' are still scored by the verifier
explanation: Section 4.4 uses the no-filter and gold arms as evidence for generic SFT damage because they decline 'with no verifier at all'. Section 5.3 repeats 'Train-on-gold, with no verifier in the loop'. The training filter is absent, but the evaluation verifier is still math-verify with the gold-storage defect, 51 unparseable golds and a \boxed-dependent extraction, as the abstract and Limitations stress ('every headline number is graded by the biased verifier'). A model trained on gold shifts to $-delimited spans and fewer boxed answers, and its measured fall can partly come from the grader. Section 4.4 does acknowledge that the verifier-error bound is lower-only and excludes the 14% unboxed generations. The 'no verifier at all' framing is still wrong for the claim it supports, and it conflicts with the paper's own scoping that all scores are verifier-graded.
related_sections: 5.3 A Proposed Audit for GVT with a Biased Verifier

title: Scoping of the 'graded by the selecting verifier' limitation is inconsistent: Abstract/Conclusion/Limitations say every score, Section 5.1 reports an independent grader
quote: and every headline number is graded by
explanation: The Abstract ('All accuracies are graded by the same verifier'), the Conclusion ('every score is graded by the selecting verifier') and Limitations ('every headline number') are absolute. Section 5.1 adds an independent string-match grader on the final-round generations, which gives the same sign and size for the −4.1 headline and the gate. The final-round headline is therefore not wholly verifier-graded, and the Abstract and Conclusion do not say so. The mitigation is also weaker than it looks: the grader keys on the last \boxed, the same extraction anchor as the verifier, and the loop's own \boxed share falls, so it does not isolate mathematics from boxing style. The paper calls it 'stricter', but stricter grading cannot recover correct answers the verifier family rejects. Section 5.1 also cites 're-scoring five runs with V′' as a mitigation, but V′ is the same math-verify with the gold wrapped, so it is not an independent grader. The final-round selection verifier (normalised gold) is also never stated to be defect-free, though the abstract says only 'Scores before the final round use the verifier with the defect'. The scope of the limitation should be stated once, consistently.
related_sections: 3.2 The Verifier and Its Directional Bias

title: Injected-bias hash control: quoted difference does not follow from the two quoted shifts
quote: the \boxed share falls 4.9 points on them and 3.1
explanation: The text says the \boxed share falls 4.9 points on affected problems and 3.1 on the others, then gives the difference as −0.1 [−6.1, 6.0]. The difference of the two falls is −1.8 (or +1.8), not −0.1. No adjustment is described (for example relative to an unbiased-run baseline). Either the numbers or the definition of the difference is wrong or missing. This matters because the paper uses this run to claim 'no selective avoidance'. A −1.8 point difference is in the avoidance direction, though the interval is wide. The content-rule run is consistent (95.0 stays vs −2.8 gives +2.8), which makes the hash-run mismatch stand out.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: Injected-bias controls are not dose-checked, contrary to the paper's own check (iii), and the 'not valid' reason in the abstract is a reporting gap
quote: and no count of avoidance examples for them.
explanation: Section 5.3 (iii) tells future work to 'Check the dose of a control before running it'. The injected-bias runs are the paper's attempt at a positive control, yet no count of training examples that could teach avoidance is given (only 49 of 300 selection problems are affected, and the pool shrinks from 298 to 263). The Abstract says the second run is invalid because it is 'a single run without rt'. That is an omission the authors could fix by computing rt from saved generations; it is not a design limitation. Section 4.6 calls the second rule 'visible' and learnable, so the power question is open rather than settled. Section 4.6 still reports 'The model does not stop boxing where boxing is penalised' as an observation, although the same paragraph says the runs cannot validate the audit. This does not meet the rigor standard the paper sets for itself. The same applies to the gate, whose dose and format behaviour are also not checked before it is treated as decisive.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe
related_sections: 5.3 A Proposed Audit for GVT with a Biased Verifier

title: Audit is both listed as a contribution and disclaimed as one
quote: and we claim neither it nor the patch control as a contribution.
explanation: Section 2 says the per-round false-reject measurement and the patch control are not claimed as contributions. The Introduction's Contributions list has a bullet 'A post hoc per-round false-reject audit of one verifier defect', followed by '(the RLVR tracking applied to offline SFT; not a novel method)'. Section 5.3 is titled 'A Proposed Audit' and presents four checks as a protocol for future studies, while the Abstract, Section 5.3 and Conclusion say that the audit is uninformative, its main readout is an identity, and it has no valid positive control. Proposing as a protocol a check whose only validation attempt failed is at odds with the disclaimers. Whether the audit is a contribution, a negative result about the audit, or a proposal should be stated consistently.
related_sections: 5.3 A Proposed Audit for GVT with a Biased Verifier

title: Train-on-gold used to calibrate rt drift 'unrelated to the verifier' despite noise-level intervals and off-distribution outputs
quote: so rt drifts by about as much as
explanation: Section 5.3 argues that rt rises of 2.1–3.3 in the gold arms show rt drifts by about as much as the observed falls 'for reasons unrelated to the verifier'. The gold-arm rt changes have intervals containing zero ([−1.2, 8.1], [−2.2, 6.7]), as do the self-training falls. The comparison is of two noise-level quantities of opposite sign, from two seeds. The gold arms also have shortened, re-styled outputs (a large shift in \boxed share and form), so the drift is not a neutral baseline for the self-training loop. rt is defined through the verifier pair (V, V′), and the audit set includes verifier-defined rejections, so 'unrelated to the verifier' is not shown. The comparison is useful as a warning about interpretability, but cannot show drift of a specific size.
source_section: 5.3 A Proposed Audit for GVT with a Biased Verifier

title: Audit (Table 5) uses all 500 problems including the 350 selection problems, the same selection-equals-evaluation weakness the paper uses to discount Design P
quote: The false-reject audit for the gold-storage defect (post hoc), in percent (all 500
explanation: Section 4.1 refuses to read Design P causally partly because 'it scores on the problems it selects from'. The Table 5 audit computes rt over all 500 problems in Design I. 350 of them are the selection problems whose accepted generations form the training pool for the next adapter, so rt there measures behaviour on problems the adapter was trained on (including the 'affected' problems with 2–12 pool examples). Accuracy tables use the 150-problem exam only. The audit never separates exam from selection problems, so memorisation of pool answers (including unboxed forms) is conflated with generalised adaptation. The paper applies a weaker standard to its own audit than it applies to Design P.
source_section: 5.3 A Proposed Audit for GVT with a Biased Verifier

title: 'Pooled decline does not reproduce under isolation' is in tension with the large declines of isolated high-rate runs
quote: A sharp pooled decline does not reproduce under isolation (Section 4.1),
explanation: Design I at 1e-5 trains on roughly 4.5 times fewer examples (872 vs 3,962), so non-reproduction there is what dose alone predicts, which the paper concedes. But isolated runs at 5e-4 show large declines: Run C pass@1 −22.0, train-on-gold −18 to −21, and −10/−11 for some A/B runs, the same order as the pooled fall of 31 points. Section 4.4 even introduces the higher rates because 1e-5 'changed the outputs little'. The claim 'does not reproduce' therefore holds only for the low-dose comparison, and the Introduction and Conclusion state it without that qualifier (only 'though dose and pooling are confounded'). Section 5.1 correctly says 'We cannot say' what produced it. The Design P / Design I comparison is also confounded by k, rounds and rate (Section 4.4), so 'reproduce' implies a matched test the study does not contain.

title: No-filter control cannot test the 'shrinking pool' explanation of Design P and comes from a different design
explanation: Section 5.2 says the shrinking-pool explanation of Design P is neither supported nor ruled out because 'the no-filter control declines without any verifier but with more dose'. The no-filter arm has a constant pool (all 1,400 samples per round), so by construction it cannot exhibit or test pool shrinkage. It is also a Design I arm with separate exam and selection sets, whereas the explanation concerns Design P with selection equal to evaluation. Using it as partial evidence about the Design P mechanism mixes designs. The argument should say the control is irrelevant to this mechanism, not 'more dose' confounded.

title: 'No consistent difference' for the no-filter control understates a consistent direction reported in Section 4.4 and Table 2
quote: Removing the ﬁlter is not better than keeping it beyond
explanation: The Abstract and 5.2 say removing the filter made 'no consistent difference'. Section 4.4 and Table 3 show pass@4 lower with no filter at both seeds (−2.0 and −5.3). Table 2 shows no-filter sample accuracy equal or worse than A (−8.2 vs −8.3; −10.2 vs −4.7) and matched finished accuracy worse in both seeds (−10.6 vs −9.1; −6.6 vs −5.5). Direction is therefore non-negative against the filter in nearly every comparison. With n=2 this is not significant, and dose is confounded as stated, but 'no consistent difference' is a stronger description than the data. Since this is the only arm that varies the verifier's role, the framing matters for the paper's second-branch discussion.
